text: operative chemoradiotherapy has produced inconsistent results, and there is insufficient evidence that it has any ad- vantage over adjuvant radiotherapy.3 In unresectable local- ly advanced disease, and in resectable disease when the aim is to avoid the need for surgery and thereby allow or- gan preservation, chemotherapy with radiotherapy is gen- erally used, and different regimens have been tried. Con- current chemoradiotherapy, without surgery, has increased survival compared with radiotherapy alone,3,4 and concur- rent treatment appears to improve overall survival more than radiotherapy with either neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy.5 Induction chemotherapy followed by con- current chemoradiotherapy has also been studied; limited data suggest that it may reduce distant failure rates and im- prove survival.3 Some therefore recommend concurrent chemoradiotherapy as the most effective treatment for cancers of the nasopharynx1,6 and larynx.1 Palliative chemotherapy is used in metastatic or recurrent disease.1,3,6 Salvage surgery or a repeat course of radio- therapy are other options, depending on previous treat- ment. Drugs used for single-agent treatment include cispl- atin, carboplatin, paclitaxel, docetaxel, fluorouracil, methotrexate, ifosfamide, bleomycin, cetuximab, and gemcitabine (for nasopharyngeal cancer). Combination regimens such as cisplatin and fluorouracil are commonly used and produce more responses, but no clear improve- ment in survival. Other common combinations include cisplatin or carboplatin with a taxane, and cisplatin plus cetuximab. The choice of best supportive care or single- agent or combination chemotherapy should be dictated by the patient’s performance status, as the benefits of chemo- therapy are limited.1 A local injection of cisplatin in a gel formulation contain- ing adrenaline has been investigated in recurrent and re- fractory head and neck cancer.7 Photodynamic therapy (see under Porfimer Sodium, p.764) using temoporfin is a more recent development for palliative management. Head and neck cancers have high levels of p53 gene mu- tations, and gene therapy is under investigation.8 Chemo- prevention by treatment of pre-malignant disease is also under investigation (see Leucoplakia, p.688). 1.
